stories.headline: Jeffco resident with measles flew in and out of Denver International Airport three times, state says
stories.summary:
A Jefferson County resident with a confirmed measles case may have exposed others at Denver International Airport and an Arvada urgent care, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment said late Thursday. The person flew in or out of DIA three times last weekend, and the agency believes the infection was likely acquired during travel rather than in Colorado.

Possible exposures at DIA occurred between 12:25 a.m. and 3 a.m. Oct. 3 (Gate C50, the airport train and an employee shuttle), between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. Oct. 4 (Gate B48), and between 11:25 p.m. Oct. 4 and 2 a.m. Oct. 5 (Gate A18). Another exposure window was at CareNow Urgent Care, 6413 Fig St. in Arvada, between 11:35 a.m. and 4:15 p.m. Oct. 7.

People exposed may develop symptoms through Oct. 28, including fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash. Anyone with symptoms should call a health care provider and report them to public health officials at 720-653-3369.

Colorado has confirmed 26 measles cases as of Oct. 15, down from 31 at this point last year. Of the 26, 22 involved people who were not vaccinated and 19 were in people younger than 18.

stories.headline: Colorado confirms first pediatric flu death of the season as cases, hospitalizations see early rise
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has confirmed the first pediatric influenza-associated death of the 2026-27 respiratory virus season. The victim was an elementary-aged child from outside the Denver metro area. State officials said Friday there is no record the child received this season's flu vaccine, and no further details were released.

The death comes as flu activity rises across Colorado, with hospitals reporting more positive flu tests and flu-related hospitalizations. The state is coming off its most severe pediatric flu season on record. In 2025-26, Colorado recorded 5,931 flu hospitalizations, the highest total since tracking began in 2004, including 1,169 involving children. Eight children died.

State epidemiologist Dr. Rachel Herlihy urged parents to vaccinate their children before transmission increases further. CDPHE recommends annual vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, and protection takes about two weeks to develop.

Vaccines are available at pharmacies, doctors' offices, community health centers and local public health agencies. Most insurance plans, including Medicaid and Child Health Plan Plus, cover the cost, and free or low-cost vaccines for uninsured children are offered at nearly 600 locations statewide.

stories.headline: Aurora leaders to vote on indefinite data center moratorium as neighbors oppose Trident data center
stories.summary:
Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman has called a special City Council meeting for 6 p.m. Monday, Oct. 19, to vote on an indefinite moratorium on new data center applications. Ward II Council Member Amy Wiles is sponsoring the proposal, which would halt acceptance of new applications until the council adopts appropriate regulations. Coffman said he fully supports it.

The moratorium has no set end date, but Coffman said applications could resume once reasonable rules are in place. Projects already in the city's system would continue to move forward, and the pause would not apply to the Trident data center that has drawn opposition from nearby residents. Wiles would lead work on how far data centers should sit from existing residential areas.

Coffman said he is pursuing other options on Trident. The current process does not require a council vote, but he said a mechanism allows him to bring it up for one, and he reserves the right to ask for a no vote.

Ray Czaplewski, who lives in The Reserve, a 55-plus community near the site, said residents learned of the project by word of mouth, with no city notice or signs. His main concern is constant low-frequency noise.

stories.headline: The Denver Post endorses Michael Allen for attorney general
stories.summary:
The Denver Post Editorial Board has endorsed Republican Michael Allen, the El Paso County district attorney, for Colorado attorney general over Democrat Jena Griswold. The board cited his integrity, his record of standing up to more extreme members of his party, and his ability to manage a large legal office and win complex criminal cases.

Allen told the board he supports some, but not all, of Attorney General Phil Weiser's lawsuits against the Trump administration. He said he would not have sued over the decision to move Space Command from Colorado Springs, calling it the wrong decision but one within the commander in chief's authority.

Allen said he would continue investigating what the editorial described as a coordinated federal attack on Colorado, citing an email discovered by Weiser's office showing Trump officials brainstorming actions against the state. He said his own 4th Judicial District was awarded about $340,000 in a federal public safety grant in 2025 but has not received the money.

The board acknowledged that Allen worked only briefly in the Kansas Attorney General's office, but said it believes he will learn quickly. It framed its endorsement as a bet on a nonpartisan approach in a hyper-partisan time.

stories.headline: Dozens of No Kings protests aimed at increasing voter participation planned across Colorado
stories.summary:
More than 70 "No Kings: Vote Early" events are scheduled Saturday across Colorado, part of more than 2,500 events planned nationwide. Unlike earlier No Kings events that targeted President Donald Trump, this round is meant to be nonpartisan and focused on encouraging people to vote early or make a voting plan before the November midterm election.

Organizers said the events cannot reference, endorse or oppose any candidates or parties. They may include block parties, rallies or walks to the polls. In Denver, people are expected to gather at the Colorado State Capitol at noon, and later in the afternoon experts will share information on statewide ballot measures in Five Points.

In Boulder, Golden and Lakewood, organizers asked attendees to bring completed ballots and march to a nearby dropbox. Other metro-area organizers encouraged attendees to drop off ballots on the way to or from the protests. In Littleton and Centennial, organizers invited participants to dress as superheroes or historical figures in a Halloween spirit.

stories.headline: Colorado's labor force shrinks to lowest participation rate since 1979
stories.summary:
Colorado's labor force lost 3,050 people in September, pulling the labor force participation rate down to 65.2%, the lowest since September 1979, according to the state Department of Labor and Employment. The state's labor force stands at about 3.18 million, down 75,000 from a year ago. The unemployment rate rose one-tenth of a point to 4.1%, versus 4.2% nationally.

Tim Wonhof, the state's labor market information director, said the decline mirrors a long-term national trend driven by an aging population and declining net migration. Workers 55 and older have nearly doubled as a share of the labor force over 25 years. Colorado still ranks ninth nationally for participation as of August.

The labor force peaked in October 2024, when it was about 95,000 larger and 67.8% of working-age Coloradans were employed or looking for work. UCCS economist Bill Craighead said the cause is hard to pin down because the state lacks data on prime-age participation and discouraged workers.

Involuntary part-time work averaged 2.6% of the labor force this year, down from 3.3% in 2025 and 5.8% in 2020.

stories.headline: Downtown Denver's revival requires more than bringing workers back, new report says
stories.summary:
A report released Thursday by the Downtown Denver Partnership says sustaining the downtown's recovery will require diversifying its economy beyond traditional office work. The report, by urban theorist Richard Florida, argues Denver could become a national model for the future of American downtowns.

Florida found foot traffic has recovered to more than 90% of pre-pandemic levels, visitor and resident activity is at or above those levels, and more people live downtown than before the pandemic. Even so, downtown has roughly 12.2 million square feet of vacant office space, nearly 11 million of it in the central business district.

Florida recommended converting offices to other uses, reinvesting in existing buildings and redeveloping properties for housing, parks and entertainment. He pointed to The Luzzatto Co.'s High Fidelity Plaza office-to-residential conversion, which obtained a $63 million low-interest loan from the Denver Downtown Development Authority.

He said activity, not office occupancy, is now the better measure of downtown health, and that by that measure the rebound is well underway.

stories.headline: Bow River Capital appoints new CEO as founder takes on new role after 23 years
stories.summary: Denver-based Bow River Capital has named Greg Hiatrides chief executive officer. The private equity firm, which manages roughly $6 billion to $7 billion, announced the change as founder Blair Richardson moves into the role of chairman after 23 years leading the firm.

stories.headline: Chinese grocery store coming to development near Denver International Airport
stories.summary:
New plans show that a development known as Tower Plaza near Denver International Airport was created specifically to add an Asian grocery store to the area. The Chinese grocery is the anchor of the project.

Two restaurants have also signed on as tenants of the development, according to the plans reported by the Denver Business Journal.

stories.headline: Frontier Airlines to cut 19 Denver routes by year-end
stories.summary:
Frontier Airlines will cut 19 routes from Denver International Airport by the end of 2026, according to a report from the Denver Business Journal carried by 9News. The reduction affects the carrier's Denver network, where it is a major operator.

Further details on which destinations are affected were not included in the available excerpt.

stories.headline: Broncos' Jonathon Cooper removed from exempt list, available to play Week 7
stories.summary:
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell removed Broncos pass-rusher Jonathon Cooper, 28, from the commissioner's exempt list, making him eligible to play in Week 7 against Arizona. Cooper had been on the list since Aug. 30 and missed Denver's first six games. The league said its review of his conduct under the personal conduct policy after two June arrests is ongoing and unaffected.

Cooper was arrested after domestic violence-related incidents involving an ex-girlfriend in June and charged with felony assault for strangulation and multiple lesser charges. His trial, originally set for next month, was moved to March 2-4.

The Broncos are off this weekend and have a one-week roster exemption, so Cooper can practice next week before being added to the 53-man roster. He could still face suspension; a six-game benchmark applies to domestic violence violations, and time already missed would count, though he would repay game checks.

His return coincides with outside linebacker Jonah Elliss suffering what appeared to be a significant right leg injury Thursday against the Seahawks.

stories.headline: Rockies fire pitching coach Alon Leichman
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies made their first offseason change Thursday by firing pitching coach Alon Leichman, according to Purple Row. As of Thursday night the team had not made the move official, and there was no word on a replacement.

The Rockies finished with the worst ERA in Major League Baseball at 5.59. The starting rotation was even worse, with a 6.28 ERA, also last in the majors.

It is too soon to know whether more coaching changes are coming.

topStory.headline: Trump Waives Key Provisions of Russia Sanctions Law Two Days Before Takeover, Drawing Bipartisan Criticism and Rebuke From Zelenskyy
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump issued an executive order Friday night waiving many of the sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia contained in a sweeping law Congress passed with bipartisan support, saying the move is "in the national interests of the United States." The law, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, was signed by Trump last month and named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. Under its terms, Trump had until Oct. 18 to impose the measures or waive them, and the administration had not told lawmakers which course it would take.

The legislation sanctions senior Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, as well as Russian banks and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to move Russian energy around existing embargoes. It also directs the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, a group that may include China and India, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the suspension "an important and truly historic moment," saying the sanctions would have caused serious damage primarily to the United States and global markets.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the decision on Saturday, calling it wrong and saying it "only helps the Russians." In a Telegram post he referred to an "American sanctions blackout" and described the weakened pressure as effectively a financial reward for Putin. He noted that overnight Russian attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities caused power cuts in several regions, saying Russia is trying to cause a blackout before winter. Zelenskyy thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the bill and praised Graham for his support of Ukraine.

Critics in Congress responded quickly. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the waivers a "craven, cowardly action" and said they had "nothing to do with our national security." Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a Ukraine supporter who is not seeking re-election, said "the president is prolonging the war, not ending it." Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., accused Trump of surrendering to Putin and defying congressional intent. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother and is running for a full term in his seat, has promoted the law as part of her campaign.

The waiver follows a deal Trump announced last week for the United States to purchase Russian diesel, with Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tons immediately, followed by additional shipments in the coming months, to ease fuel prices that have risen roughly 70% since the war in Iran began in February. A bipartisan group of a dozen senators, including six Republicans, had sent a letter urging Trump to rescind the diesel deal and to carry out the sanctions authorities. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have grown strained, with Trump criticizing Zelenskyy publicly, saying he is harder to deal with than Putin, and expressing frustration with Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. With midterm elections less than three weeks away and the cost of living a leading concern for voters, the dispute is likely to continue in Congress, where lawmakers from both parties have signaled opposition to the decision.
